BOSTON (1848–1854)

Peter Chardon Brooks, the other grandfather, died on the first day of 1849, leaving what was thought the largest estate in Boston—some two million dollars—to his seven surviving children: four sons, Edward, Peter Chardon, Gorham, and Sydney; and three daughters—Charlotte, married to Edward Everett; Ann, to Nathaniel Frothingham, minister of the First Church; and Abigail Brown, born April 25, 1808, married September 3, 1829, to Charles Francis Adams, hardly a year older than herself. Their first child, in 1830, was a daughter, Louisa Catherine; the second, a son, John Quincy; the third took his father’s name, Charles Francis; the fourth, of less account, fell in a way to his mother, who named him Henry Brooks, after a favorite brother just lost. Others followed, but these elder four bore the brunt of what their elders still called education.

The Adams connection in Boston was singularly small, the Brooks family singularly large and, for the place, brilliant—almost wholly of clerical New England stock, steeped in the habit of sermon and self-respect. One might have sought long, even in older societies, for three brothers-in-law more distinguished than Edward Everett, Dr. Frothingham, and Mr. Adams; and equally long for seven brothers-in-law more unlike. They bore the stamp of Massachusetts Bay, but the shades of difference were contrasts. Everett, among the most ambitious Bostonians, had early broken bounds—leaving the Unitarian pulpit for Congress—had supported J. Q. Adams’s administration; the social consequence was the marriage that bound Everett’s house to the President’s son. Jackson’s wreck of parties had wrecked many careers, Everett’s among them, but the Whig tide had lifted him to the English Mission and brought him home with a European halo—undisputed rank next only to Webster as Boston’s representative figure. Dr. Frothingham belonged to the same clerical school, less clerical in manner. With either, Mr. Adams had little in common—he was younger, deeply biassed by his father, and by the inherited feud between Quincy and State Street; yet personal relations were friendly enough as far as a boy could see, and the innumerable cousins went, winters, to the First Church and slept through their uncle’s sermons without once asking what they meant for them. For two hundred years the First Church had harbored such little boys, sleeping more or less soundly under the same feuds; and the feuds still smouldered.

Death had cleared the score of 1812. The quarrels of John Adams and John Quincy Adams were no longer acutely personal; the game stood as drawn; Charles Francis Adams, in due succession to Webster and Everett, might have taken the inherited leadership. Between him and State Street the relation was more natural than between Everett and State Street; but he drew aloof and renewed the old war that had lasted since 1700. He could not help it. With J. Q. Adams’s record fresh in memory, his only representative could not make terms with the slave-power that overshadowed Boston’s great interests. Even his children—who had as yet no principles—could as little follow Webster or Seward. They would have lost in consideration more than they could gain in patronage. They were anti-slavery by birth, as their name was Adams and their home was Quincy. State Street would never trust them; nor they it. Had State Street been Paradise, they must hunger vainly for it; and it hardly needed Daniel Webster to act as archangel with the flaming sword and order them from the door.

Time taught the boy gentler judgment, but, at ten, his face was already fixed, his heart stone, against State Street; his education warped beyond recovery toward Puritan politics. Between him and his patriot grandfather at the same age, the conditions had changed little. The year 1848 was like enough to 1776 to make a fair parallel. The stamp of 1848 was almost as indelible as 1776, and for boys whose lives should fall between 1865 and 1900, the first task was to get rid of it. That was their education. Outsiders and adventurers might find it easy; the old Puritan nature rebelled. Its reason was forcible: it held its thought higher and its moral standards better than those of its successors—so they were—and could not be convinced that moral standards had nothing to do with it; that utilitarian morality was good enough for the graceless. Nature had given the boy a character that, in any former century, would have led him into the Church; he inherited dogma and a priori habit from the beginning of time; and needed no violent reaction like anti-slavery politics to sweep him back into Puritanism with the violence of a religious war.

His education, to this point, was inheritance. For the next five or six years, his father alone counted. If he were to worry safely through life’s quicksands, he must depend on his father’s pilotage; but the father’s channel lay clear—his task was to get by the dangers of the slave-power, or fix its bounds; once done, he might be content to let his sons pay for the pilotage, with their lives wasted on battle-fields, or in misdirected energies and lost opportunity. The generation that lived from 1840 to 1870 could do very well with the old forms; that which had its work to do between 1870 and 1900 needed something quite new.

Hence, the son became an interested critic of his father’s mind and temper. Long after, as old men, the brothers still discussed it. To Henry, the trait that distinguished his father from all the others of the name was, simply, that he possessed the only perfectly balanced mind the name had produced. For a hundred years newspaper scribblers derided or abused the older Adamses for want of judgment. They abused Charles Francis for his judgment. The traits were real. He was singular for mental poise—absence of self-assertion or self-consciousness—the faculty of standing apart without seeming aware that he was alone; a balance of mind and temper that neither challenged nor avoided notice; that admitted no question of superiority or inferiority, jealousy, or personal motive, even under pressure. Ripened by age, this poise became more striking as the son learned to measure the mental faculties themselves, which were in no way exceptional for depth or range. His memory stood hardly above the average; his mind was not bold like his grandfather’s, or restless like his father’s; not imaginative or oratorical—still less mathematical; but it worked with singular perfection, admirable self-restraint, instinctive mastery of form. Within its range it was a model.

Boston’s standards were high—much affected by the old clerical self-respect that gave the Unitarian clergy unusual charm—Channing, Everett, Frothingham, Palfrey, Walker, Emerson, and their allies would have commanded distinction anywhere. Yet the Adamses had little affinity with the pulpit, and less with its eccentric offshoots—Parker, Brook Farm, Concord philosophy. Boston’s literary group—Ticknor, Prescott, Longfellow, Motley, Holmes—was strong, but Mr. Adams was not one of them; they were, as a rule, too Websterian. Science had its eminence, especially in medicine, and Mr. Adams cared little for science. He stood alone. He had no master—hardly even his father. He had no scholars—hardly even his sons.

Almost alone among his Boston contemporaries, he was not English in sympathies. Perhaps a hundred years of acute hostility to England had bred the family trait; with him it went further—indifference to social distinction. Never once in forty years did his son see in him a trace of snobbishness. An English duke or duchess left him indifferent; royalty itself was only a slightly inconvenient presence. He had every reason to affect the manner of a courtier; he never showed it. Never did his son see him flatter or vilify, envy or be jealous; never a shade of vanity; never a tone of arrogance; never a gesture of pride.

The same might perhaps have been said of John Quincy Adams; but in him, his associates averred, it was accompanied by mental restlessness and a lamentable want of judgment. No one charged Charles Francis with this fault; they charged him with the opposite—coldness. No doubt perfect poise was not maintained without sacrifice of the qualities that upset it. His children, restless-minded, introspective, self-conscious, were too ignorant of the world to suspect how rare and complete was the model before them. A coarser instrument would have impressed them more. Average human nature is coarse; its ideals must be average. The world never loved perfect poise. It loves the absence of poise; it must be amused. Napoleons and Andrew Jacksons amuse it; perfect balance does not. Had his nature been cold, he would have followed Webster, Everett, Seward, Winthrop, in party discipline and self-interest. Had it been less balanced, he would have gone with Garrison, Phillips, Edmund Quincy, and Parker into secession. Between the two paths he found an intermediate one—distinctive and characteristic—he set up a party of his own.

This party became a chief influence in the boy’s education from 1848 to 1854, violently affecting character when it is plastic. The group—whose social centre was Mount Vernon Street—numbered three: Dr. John G. Palfrey, Richard H. Dana, and Charles Sumner. Palfrey, the eldest, though of clerical education, was, to a boy, often the most agreeable; his talk was lighter, his range wider; he had wit, or humor, and the give-and-take of the dinner table; born for a man of the world, he forced himself to be clergyman, professor, statesman, while yearning, like every true Bostonian, for the Athenæum Club or a Combination Room. Dana at first seemed the opposite—still before the mast, bluff, vigorous; only later did one find a man of excessive refinement forcing himself to work like a day-laborer, hardening his skin to the burden, as though still carrying hides at Monterey. Undoubtedly he succeeded; his mind and will were robust; but he might have echoed his lifelong friend William M. Evarts: “I pride myself on my success in doing not the things I like to do, but the things I don’t like to do.” His ideal was to be a great Englishman, on the front benches until promoted to the woolsack; above all, with a social status to lift him above provincial annoyance; but he took life as it came, suffocating longings with grim self-discipline. Of the four, Dana was the most marked; never dogmatic or self-asserting, he always filled his space; and, disguise it as he would, he was aristocratic to the tenth generation.

In that respect—and that only—Sumner was like him; in all else he stood out of line. He adored English standards, but his ambition rivalled Edmund Burke. No Bostonian had made a more brilliant start—rather in Edward Everett’s steps than Webster’s. As an orator he had triumphed by his oration against war; Boston admired him chiefly for social success in England and on the Continent—a halo never bestowed by domestic sanctity. By interest and instinct he felt the value of English connection, and cultivated it the more as politics made him an outcast in Boston society. He was rarely without a pocketful of letters from duchesses and noblemen. Having sacrificed to principle his position in America, he clung to foreign attachments. The Free Soil Party fared ill on Beacon Street; the social arbiters—George Ticknor and the rest—had to admit that its leaders could not mingle with Webster’s friends. Sumner was ostracized; so were Palfrey, Dana, Russell, Adams, and the rest; but they had houses and families; Sumner had neither wife nor household. Though the most socially ambitious and the hungriest for polite society, he could enter hardly half a dozen houses. Longfellow stood by him in Cambridge; in Beacon Street he found refuge at Mr. Lodge’s; yet his solitude was glacial and reacted on character: he had nothing but himself to think about. His superiority was real; he was the classical ornament of the anti-slavery party; their pride and admiration were unbounded.

The boy worshipped him; if he ever regarded any older man as a personal friend, it was Sumner. The relation in the household was closer than any tie of blood; none of the uncles approached it. Sumner was the boy’s model of greatness; nature and art combined. The only fault of such a model was its superiority, which defied imitation. To a twelve-year-old, Palfrey, Dana, his father, were men he might become; Sumner belonged to another order—heroic.

As the boy turned ten or twelve, his father gave him a writing-table in an alcove of the Boston library; winter after winter he worked at his Latin Grammar and listened to these four discussing the course of anti-slavery politics. The discussions were always serious; the Free Soil Party took itself seriously; and they were habitual because Mr. Adams had undertaken a newspaper—the organ of these gentlemen—who came to discuss policy and expression. At the same time he was editing the Works of his grandfather, John Adams, and made the boy read texts for proof-correction. In later years the father complained that, as a reader of Novanglus and Massachusettensis, Henry showed little consciousness of punctuation; the boy took it as warning—if ever he grew up to write dull discussions, to be dull in a different way from his great-grandfather. Yet the discussions in the Boston Whig were carried on in much the same style, and appealed to much the same habit of mind. The boy got as little education, fit for his own time, from one as from the other, and no more from the gentlemen themselves, who were types of the past.

Down to 1850, New England society was still directed by the professions. Lawyers, physicians, professors, merchants were classes, acting as though each profession were a church. In politics the system required competent expression; government by the best, Ciceronian fashion, had produced the long line of New England statesmen. They chose men to be well represented, and chose the best they had. Thus Boston chose Daniel Webster, and Webster took—not pay, but honorarium—the cheques raised for him by Peter Harvey from Appletons, Perkinses, Amorys, Searses, Brookses, Lawrences, and so on, who begged him to represent them. Everett held rank in succession to Webster; Winthrop claimed succession to Everett; Sumner aspired to break the succession but not the system. The Adamses had never long been part of this State succession; they preferred national service and won all their distinction there; but they, too, had required State support and commonly received it. The Mount Vernon Street group was an offshoot of this system; statesmen, not politicians; guiding public opinion, little guided by it.

The boy learned one lesson from breathing such air: that this world—the same that had always existed in Boston—was the world he was to fit. Had he known Europe, he would have learned no better. Paris of Louis Philippe, Guizot, and de Tocqueville; London of Peel, Macaulay, and Mill were varieties of the same upper-class bourgeoisie that felt cousinship with Boston of Ticknor, Prescott, and Motley. Even Carlyle, grumbling at the middle class and posing as eccentric, found friendship at Boston and Concord. The system seemed so successful that Germany wanted to try it; Italy yearned for it. England’s middle-class government was the ideal of human progress. The violent reaction after 1848, and Europe’s return to military practices, never shook true faith. No one, save Karl Marx, foresaw radical change. What announced it? The world produced sixty or seventy million tons of coal; used near a million steam-horsepower, just beginning to make itself felt. All experience since the creation of man, all revelation or human science, conspired to deceive a twelve-year-old boy who took for granted that his respectable ideas would be respected.

Viewed from Mount Vernon Street, life’s problem was simple and classic. Politics offered no difficulties; there the moral law was a sure guide. Social perfection was sure, because human nature worked for Good, and three instruments were all she asked—Suffrage, Common Schools, and Press. Doubt was forbidden. Education was divine; man needed only a correct knowledge of facts to reach perfection:

“Were half the power that fills the world with terror,
Were half the wealth bestowed on camps and courts,
Given to redeem the human mind from error,
There were no need of arsenals nor forts.”

Nothing quieted doubt like the mental calm of the Unitarian clergy. In uniform excellence of life and character, moral and intellectual, the score of Unitarian clergymen who controlled society and Harvard were never excelled. They insisted on no doctrine; they taught the means of leading a virtuous, useful, unselfish life—sufficient for salvation. Difficulties might be ignored; doubts were waste; nothing exacted solution. Boston had solved the universe—or offered and realized the best solution yet tried. The problem was worked out.

Of all the conditions of youth that afterwards puzzled the man, this disappearance of religion puzzled him most. The boy went to church twice every Sunday; he was taught to read his Bible; he learned religious poetry by heart; he believed in a mild deism; he prayed; he went through the forms; but neither to him nor to his brothers or sisters was religion real. Even the mild discipline of the Unitarian Church was so irksome that they all threw it off at the first possible moment, and never afterwards entered a church. That the most powerful emotion of man, next to the sexual, should disappear might be a personal defect; but that the most intelligent society, led by the most intelligent clergy, in the most moral conditions he ever knew, should have so solved the universe as to cease anxiety about past or future; should persuade itself that the problems which had convulsed human thought from earliest time were not worth discussion, seemed the most curious social phenomenon he had to account for. The faculty of turning away one’s eyes as one approaches a chasm is not unusual, and Boston showed, under Mr. Webster’s lead, how successfully it could be done in politics; there, at least, some protested. In religion and philosophy no one protested. Such protest as appeared took simpler forms than the silence—Theodore Parker’s deism, and that of the boy’s cousin, Octavius Frothingham, distressed the father and scandalized Beacon Street by avowing scepticism that seemed to solve no old problems and raise many new. Emerson’s less aggressive protest was, from an old-world point of view, naïf.

Thus the children reached manhood without religion, certain that dogma, metaphysics, abstract philosophy were not worth knowing. So one-sided an education could have been possible in no other time or country; it became, almost of necessity, literary and political. They joined the dinner-table debates; from childhood the boys heard table-talk as good as they were ever to hear again. The eldest, Louisa, was one of the most sparkling creatures her brother met in a long experience of bright women. John, the oldest son, became one of the best talkers in Boston and perhaps the most popular man in the State, though apt to be on the unpopular side. Palfrey and Dana could be entertaining at will; Sumner could hardly be called light in hand, but he was willing to be amused, and smiled grandly from time to time; while Mr. Adams, who talked relatively little, was always a good listener, and laughed over a witticism till he choked.

Meanwhile the stamp of 1848 set the direction of his boyish path. A few months after John Quincy Adams’s death, a convention at Buffalo met to organize a new party and named for President, Martin Van Buren; for Vice-President, Charles Francis Adams. For any American boy the fact that his father was running for office dwarfed all other excitements; but even apart from bias, 1848 fixed the road for twenty years. There was no side-path of escape. The Puritan, thinking his thought higher and his standards better, balked at change; the boy’s nature—fit for the Church in an earlier age—took, under the stress, the tone of a religious war; his father’s pilotage seemed to suffice for the voyage in sight; beyond, an unknown ocean waited.

He learned to distrust the lecture and put his faith in the talk—not because either taught him what he should need after 1870, but because the talk was alive and the lecture dead. By early youth he distrusted schoolrooms and drifted toward self-instruction in family libraries and talk; the lecture would always bore him and the independent reading lure him.
